extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, correspondents, copy-readers, and compositors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style-book rules for preparing, marking, and punctuating newspaper copy (handling longhand/typewritten copy, page/insert conventions) and detailed punctuation/capitalization/abbreviation rules for news writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of copy / consult the style-book
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy is any manuscript prepared for printing and is written according to the individual style rules of each newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first thing for a reporter to do on beginning work in an office is to ask for the style-book, the manual for the guidance of reporters, copy-readers, and compositors. If the paper has no printed rules, study the paper's columns and changes made in your own stories; if the paper does have a manual, write stories as nearly as possible in accord with the printed rules, because copy readers will insist on strict observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typewriter proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must know how to handle a typewriter dexterously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In all offices reporters are furnished typewriters and are helpless until they learn to use the machine; longhand copy is rarely sent to compositors and is usually typed by stenographers or reporters before dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longhand copy legibility and special marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When forced to write in longhand, write with painstaking care for accuracy and legibility; mark unusual names/letters to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print unusual proper names letter by letter. If letters may be confused (e.g., n vs u, a vs o), underscore/overscore as directed. Use half-circle quotation-marks to show beginning/end; use a small cross or circle to indicate a period if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use unglazed paper of a neutral tint and appropriate size and firmness for copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper does not supply stationery, choose unglazed neutral-tint paper (gray, yellow, manila brown), commonly unruled print paper 6x9 or 8½x11 inches, firm enough for ink or pencil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins and first page top space
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave specific margins and top-of-first-page space so headlines and corrections can be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top half of first page should be left blank (headline space). All sheets should have 1-inch margins at bottom and each side; all sheets except the first should have 1-inch top margin. Side margins are for corrections; bottom margins for pasting; top margins for paging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph indentation and marking
rubrics_metrics.description: Indent all paragraphs (including the first) one inch and mark with the paragraph sign; use paragraph symbol conventions for separations and completions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indent irrespective of where preceding paragraph ended and mark with the paragraph sign (a rectangle) before the first word. If paragraphs need separation, insert the paragraph symbol immediately before the new paragraph and repeat in the margin. Put a paragraph sign at the end when the paragraph completes the page to indicate compositor handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of paragraphs (marking runs and joins)
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining or joining paragraphs or lines, indicate continuity with lines and 'No' marks so compositors know to run text together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw a line from the end of the first to the start of the second and mark 'No ^' in the margin when consolidating paragraphs written separately. To join lines or remove unnecessary indent, draw a line to the left margin and mark 'No If'. Use diagonal lines across page-end and next-page starts to indicate continuation across pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crowded lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not crowd lines; use triple spaces for typewritten copy and leave quarter-inch between longhand lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowded lines force copy-readers to cut and paste. Exception: slightly crowd last lines of a page rather than run a few words to the next page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page handling (one side only, numbering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write on both sides of sheets; number pages with Arabic numerals enclosed in a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write on more than one side; in big dailies sheets are cut into takes and sent to different compositors. Number new pages at the top with arabic numerals enclosed in a circle to prevent confusion with the article text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insertions (cut-and-paste method)
rubrics_metrics.description: For considerable additions or insertions, cut the page and paste in the addition rather than writing in margins or on separate sheets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fold the lower edge forward upon the written page to match length of other sheets; do not fold backward (may be unnoticed).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Add' stories and insert/slug conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Add' stories (follow-ups) and inserts must be clearly marked with catch lines, numbers, and slugging to indicate placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When story is incomplete write 'More' in a circle at foot. Mark additions like 'Add 1. Saloon Robbery', second 'Add 2, Saloon Robbery'. An insert is 'Insert A, Saloon Robbery' with precise place indicated (e.g., 'Insert after first paragraph of lead'). Enclose such directions in rings so compositor does not set them into story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations and clippings placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate approximate placement of cuts/illustrations and paste clippings into copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Turn rule for cut' to indicate where to make a black ruled line in proofs for later insertion of a cut; make-up editor may move it. Always paste clippings—do not use pins or clips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underscoring conventions for type
rubrics_metrics.description: Use underscoring to indicate type emphasis: once for italics, twice for SMALL CAPITALS, three times for CAPITALS; wave-line for display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many papers lack italic/small-cap types; reword instead of underscoring for emphasis when necessary. Example: underscore once = italics. Use wave-line for display type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections markup conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific visible marks to indicate corrections, transpositions, restores, spelling-out figures, and intentional nonstandard text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike out words with a line through them and draw a line between words to be set together. Restore wrongly stricken word by dots beneath and write 'stet' in margin. Indicate transposition by a line over the first and under the second and write 'tr' in margin. Indicate change of case by drawing a line downward from right to left. Enclose in a circle a figure or abbreviation to indicate it should be spelled out. For deliberate slang/misspellings/ungrammatical text to be set as-is, put 'Follow Copy' in margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: End mark and final handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark story completion with a clear end mark and hand copy to city editor unfolded if possible; read carefully for errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an end mark like a # or the telegrapher's sign. Read every page carefully correcting every error; do not roll copy, do not pin sheets together; fold lengthwise only if necessary (not crosswise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare printed story to your copy
rubrics_metrics.description: After the story appears in print, read it against your copy to detect errors and learn editorial expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping carbon copies and comparing word-for-word lets a reporter change style for the better and learn what is expected at the city desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation importance and general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough knowledge of general punctuation rules (capitals, commas, dashes, parentheses, etc.) is practically a necessity; bad punctuation is worse than bad spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rules that follow are general guidelines for news writers; remember papers have their own rules but these are fundamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization: proper names and general categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper names (persons, places, things) and specific categorical items with defined exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes detailed subrules (titles of books — capitalize first and important words; names/titles of Deity — capitalize; names of Bible and sacred books — capitalize, but not adjectives derived from them; titles of respect/honor — capitalize when immediately preceding names; names indicating nationality/locality; athletic teams; festivals and holidays; societies/parties/organizations; ordinal numbers for sessions/wards; names of buildings/squares/parks; common nouns joined with proper names — capitalize when preceding; do not capitalize boards/committees when standing alone; prefixes von/de/etc. are not capitalized except sentence-initially; toasts — capitalize important words; nouns followed by numerals — do not capitalize the noun; Resolutions for Debate — capitalize 'Resolved' and 'That' following).

rubrics_metrics.name: The period: roman numerals, abbreviations, contractions, side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when to use periods: omit after roman numerals; place periods after certain abbreviations and initials; do not use for contractions; put a period after side-heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Louis XIV (no period); use period in 'Wm., Thos., Ph.D.'; do not put a period after contracted words or nicknames (Bill, Tom); side-heads and figures at beginnings of paragraphs take a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: The colon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to introduce formal quotations and formal enumerations, in time indications, and generally when the following explains what precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: introduce a formal quotation with a colon; use a colon before lists of dead or injured; use colon between hours and minutes (2:30); use colon when the following clause explains the preceding clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: The semicolon usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use semicolons to separate independent clauses lacking connectives, in complex lists (e.g., where town/residence follows names), and between teams and scores in athletic results; semicolons may replace commas when clause internal commas cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note editorial trend toward avoiding semicolons by making separate sentences; examples given for permissible and better alternatives; use semicolons in lists of names with towns (Allen Rogers of Los Vegas, N. M.; Orren Thomas of Benton, Mo.; etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: The comma usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas to set off parenthetic expressions, words in apposition, before 'namely'/'that is' etc., contrasted words, introductory words/phrases, direct address, explanatory dates/names, and academic/honorary titles; use in series, after interjections, with short quotations, to separate large numbers into groups of three, in athletic scores (between team and score), in biblical passages (chapter, verse), and in 'Resolved, That' constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt about need for a comma, omit it. Prefer clarity; example: 'The teller was kicked, beaten, and robbed by four masked men.' Use commas sparingly — only when a distinct pause or clarity demands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: The dash usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dash to mark sudden suspension/break in thought, between dateline and story start, after 'namely' when introducing an example, between office and officer in lists of officers, between Q./A. or speaker and statement in dialogue/Q&A, and to indicate slowness/hesitancy in speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a new paragraph for each speaker in quoted Q&A; examples provided for dateline use: 'Sylvester, Ga., Jan. 21. — Five negroes...' and for slowness: 'These, he said, were his — er — wife's slippers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose party/state/county names in parentheses in legislative/congressional reports; generally avoid parentheses within sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Mr. Smith (Dem., S.C.)'. Prefer breaking a sentence into two rather than using internal parenthetic clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation-marks rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation-marks for direct quotations; internal quotations use single marks; multi-paragraph quotations get opening quotes at each paragraph but closing only at the last; omit quotation marks if the quotation is set in smaller type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mix direct quotation and condensed summary in the same paragraph—use separate paragraphs. Enclose titles of books/plays/songs/poems in quotation marks. Do not quote names of newspapers, magazines, paintings, vessels, cars, or animals. Enclose slang/technical terms unfamiliar to reader in quotes. Do not quote nicknames of persons or characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe rules (possessive & contractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use apostrophe + s for singular possessive (even if word ends in s); use apostrophe + s for plural possessives not ending in s; use only apostrophe for plurals ending in s; possessive pronouns have no apostrophe; use apostrophe to mark contractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Burns's house, men's meeting, ladies' outfitter. In joint names, place apostrophe after nearest name (Farmers and Merchants' bank, Allen and Bowen's 'Classical Mythology').

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and compound-word conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate members of compound words and specific prefix/suffix combinations; list of commonly hyphenated compounds is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphenate words compounded with prefixes/suffixes like brother-, cross-, ex-, full-, half-, president-elect, mother-in-law, etc. Use wave of examples provided; follow machine/type capabilities (some papers lack italic/small cap types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words written solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain compounds with specified prefixes/suffixes are written solid (no hyphen); list of common solid compounds provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefixes include a-, after-, auto-, inter-, intra-, mid-, mis-, non-, over-, post-, re-, sub-, super-, un-, under-, up- etc. Examples: anyone, baseball, newcomer, typewriter, northward, upstairs, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words written separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Some compound expressions are written as two separate words; list provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'all right', 'back yard', 'half dollar', 'police court', 'any time', 'pro tem', 'some one' (older formulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound numbers hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound numbers between twenty and one hundred, when spelled out, should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twenty-one, forty-three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word division (end-of-line hyphenation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing a word at the end of a line, follow detailed rules to avoid breaking syllables or creating awkward or misleading divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not break a syllable incorrectly; do not divide monosyllables; do not separate consonant from vowel that affects pronunciation; do not divide diphthongs or separate successive vowels where one is silent; do not separate an added 's' syllable; do not divide hyphenated words except at regular hyphen; avoid awkward divisions; do not begin a line with a hyphen; avoid dividing a word at the end of a page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations: general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, avoid abbreviations; typewriters have encouraged writing out words in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writing words fully unless conventional abbreviations are customary or required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations of personal and professional titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain personal and professional titles may be abbreviated when preceding proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowable abbreviations include Adjt. Gen., Brig. Gen., Capt., Col., Dr., Gov., Hon., Lieut., Mr., Mrs., Prof., Rev., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of titles (rules for Mr./Mrs./Prof./Rev., etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific usage rules govern when to use Mr./Mrs./Prof./titles before names, when to omit, and how to list groups of women or couples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use Mr. before a man's name when his baptismal name or initials are given (use 'A. B. Crayton'). After initial mention, omit initials and use Mr. or a title thereafter (Prof. O. C. Bowen ... Prof. Bowen). If a person has multiple titles, use the highest rank or the one best known. Use 'Mrs.' before married women's names and 'Miss' before unmarried. For lists of unmarried women, use 'Misses'; lists of married women may use 'Mesdames' though 'Mrs.' before each is preferred. When mentioning a man and his wife use 'Mr. and Mrs. William Black' (not 'William Black and wife'). Do not use 'Master' for a boy. Before 'Rev.' put 'the' (the Rev. T. P. Frost); if initials unknown write 'the Rev. Mr. Frost.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Months and states abbreviation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for when months and states may be abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate month names (except March, April, May, June, July) when followed by a numeral indicating day (Sept. 18), but do not abbreviate when month stands alone. Abbreviate state names when preceded by a town or city (Pueblo, Col.; Manila, P.I.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Miscellaneous allowed and forbidden abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of miscellaneous permissible abbreviations and forbidden abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible: Esq., Inc., Jr., A.B., Ph.D., M.D., U.S.N., etc., when used after proper names; a.m., p.m., A.D., B.C. when preceded by numerals. Forbidden on most newspapers: abbreviations of Christian names (Chas. for Charles), Mount/Fort/Saint (Mt., Ft., St.), railroad/company/brothers abbreviations (R. R., Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers and dates formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for date/numerical formatting in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write year dates always in figures (1916). Write month dates in figures when preceded by the name of the month (July 7, 1916); when the month name does not precede, spell out the date ('the tenth'). Do not write 'the 25th of December' — use 'Dec. 25.'
